awd_titl_txt: Doctoral Dissertation Research: Intestinal energy absorption among children living in poor sanitary conditions
awd_abstract_narration:
In order to remain healthy and to grow, children need to consume a diet with sufficient energy. Food’s energy, however, is only made available for the body’s metabolic functions through intestinal absorption, which is impacted by both environmental and evolutionary factors. For example, children living in adverse and unsanitary conditions often have damaged intestines and poor intestinal energy absorption, which negatively affects their growth, development, and lifelong metabolic health. Impaired intestinal absorption leads to increased energy loss through urine and feces. This loss causes higher food energy demands, that may not be attainable under adverse conditions. Despite its importance, research and data on intestine function variation and its impact on children’s health and growth is limited. To address this issue, this doctoral dissertation research project investigates differences in children’s energy absorption among those living in adverse and unsanitary conditions in both rural and peri-urban contexts. Results are shared broadly, and outreach activities are directed to K-12 children.  

This research advances understanding of the role of intestinal absorption in driving variation in human phenotype and health by investigating intestinal function among children living in rural and peri-urban contexts. Data collection in both contexts capture a wide range of variation in experienced diet, lifestyle, sanitation, and pathogen exposure. There are two main research questions: (1) How do household conditions relate to children’s intestinal function and energy loss? And (2) How do intestinal function and energy loss impact children’s body size and nutritional status? By measuring fecal energy loss using the 'bomb' calorimetry approach, this research has the potential to better characterize global variation in intestinal energy absorption and to improve the accuracy of estimates of children’s energy requirements. These improved estimates will refine life history models of human evolution and could inform more effective nutritional interventions for children in similar contexts.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Outcomes Report

The ability to extract energy from food is fundamental to survival, growth, and reproduction and has almost certainly been under strong selective pressure throughout human evolution. Yet, despite its central role in human biology, intestinal energy absorption has received remarkably little attention at the population level (outside of clinical contexts). Addressing this gap is particularly important given growing evidence that environmentally driven intestinal impairment is a key contributor to growth faltering among children globally. 

This project used an interdisciplinary perspective and integrated field- and lab-based approach to investigate intestinal energy absorption among school-age Indigenous Shuar children of Amazonian Ecuador. It addressed two primary questions: (1) How do household environmental conditions relate to intestinal function and intestinal energy loss among children? (2) How does variation in intestinal function and energy loss influences children's body size and nutritional status?

Project Intellectual Merit

This project addressed a largely unexplored aspect of human energetics and represents the first investigation of intestinal energy absorption among children living in a low-resource setting, outside of clinical contexts. Using bomb calorimetry, the gold standard method for quantifying intestinal energy absorption, this project provides some of the first measurements of intestinal energy absorption among children. Intestinal energy absorption was found to vary by hundreds of calories a day among school-age Shuar children, with males absorbing more calories from food than females. Moreover, markers of intestinal inflammation were positively related to reduced energy absorption. These findings indicate that sub-clinical levels of intestinal inflammation may compromise the efficiency with which children extract calories from food. Another key finding was that children with higher intestinal energy absorption also exhibited higher attained height-for-age, indicating implications for growth and nutritional status. These key findings suggest that intestinal energy absorption varies widely, it is reduced with intestinal inflammation and may represent an overlooked pathway linking intestinal dysfunction to childhood growth faltering in unsanitary contexts. 

Understanding variation in intestinal energy absorption is crucial for accurately determining individual energy requirements, as some individuals may absorb more or less energy from the same foods. As such, this project opens new opportunities for understanding energy requirements at both the individual and population levels. By investigating how intestinal energy absorption varies among children, the project provides a foundation for future research and interventions aimed at addressing nutritional requirements in contexts of malnutrition and intestinal dysfunction. Consequently, this work not only advances anthropological and human biological research but also provides valuable insights for related disciplines, including nutritional science and public health.

Project Broader Impacts

This project has resulted in a number of broader impacts. It provided substantial interdisciplinary training, mentorship, and professional development for the co-PI. This included STEM training in gold-standard techniques, such as mass spectrometry (for the assessment of intestinal permeability and absorption using the lactulose:mannitol test) and bomb calorimetry (for the assessment of intestinal energy absorption). These activities were essential for the successful completion of the co-PI’s doctoral research and professional training. The project also provided hands-on STEM training for one undergraduate and two graduate students (all women from traditionally underrepresented groups).

Findings will continue to be disseminated to local and international health workers, researchers and collaborators. These data are rare and have the potential to inform efforts to more accurately estimate child energy requirements in Shuar communities and identify factors that increase the risk of intestinal dysfunction and energy malabsorption in children. The findings may also contribute to broader efforts to address environmentally driven intestinal dysfunction and growth faltering in low-resource settings. Finally, during data collection, participating families, children and school authorities were provided with information on optimal sanitary practices (e.g., water treatment), nutrition, and basic health indicators, including growth and nutritional status. These activities promise to increase awareness of health and sanitation practices and provide benefits to participating communities.
